coredata.dc:description: The proposed research intended to acquire the perception of proficient biomethane generation enhanced by TiO2 embedded chitosan thin film (TCTF) mediated enzyme secreting bacterial pretreatment of sludge. Impregnates 0.05 g/g SS TiO2 dosage on chitosan solid matrix effectively disperse sludge flocs and induces deflocculation of 99.35%. This TCTF enhances the enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration by increasing the hydrolytic activity. A higher solubilisation of 16% achieved in TCTF mediated bacterial disintegration while related to enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration alone. The high specific growth rate of 0.2 h−1 for enzyme secreting bacterial growth rate is attained at 42 h. Deflocculation and enzyme secreting bacterial pretreatment has a major impact on methane potential assay. The sludge sample TCTF mediated bacterial disintegration yields 140.40 mL/g COD higher methane than the other samples. The energetic and cost analysis of the proposed work confirms the feasibility of this sludge management process having profitable net cost of 89.92 USD/Ton of sludge.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The proposed research intended to acquire the perception of proficient biomethane generation enhanced by TiO2 embedded chitosan thin film (TCTF) mediated enzyme secreting bacterial pretreatment of sludge. Impregnates 0.05 g/g SS TiO2 dosage on chitosan solid matrix effectively disperse sludge flocs and induces deflocculation of 99.35%. This TCTF enhances the enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration by increasing the hydrolytic activity. A higher solubilisation of 16% achieved in TCTF mediated bacterial disintegration while related to enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration alone. The high specific growth rate of 0.2 h−1 for enzyme secreting bacterial growth rate is attained at 42 h. Deflocculation and enzyme secreting bacterial pretreatment has a major impact on methane potential assay. The sludge sample TCTF mediated bacterial disintegration yields 140.40 mL/g COD higher methane than the other samples. The energetic and cost analysis of the proposed work confirms the feasibility of this sludge management process having profitable net cost of 89.92 USD/Ton of sludge.

ce:section.ce:para: In recent times, the wastewater treatment sectors emancipate waste activated sludge (WAS) which need effectual treatment prior to disposal due to the existence of high harmful pathogens, organic chemicals and other inorganic inert substances [1]. Improper disposal of organic-rich WAS leads to health effects, pollution and contamination to the bionetwork. Sludge management is tedious and expensive since it consumes 60% operational cost of overall wastewater treatment plant and faces constraints due to strict law [2,3]. Hence, energy and cost-efficient anaerobic digestion process meets the energy demand and enriches the solid reduction for safe disposal of organic WAS.

The bioenergy production from WAS is deemed as an essential process intent to recycle, reduce and reuse of available high suspended and bio-accumulated organics [4]. Even though anaerobic degradation of sludge has gained more attention during the past decades but its potency is limited due to inefficient lengthy hydrolysis step. This devours digestion time due to complex floc structure that impedes higher organic utilization for proficient methane yield [5]. To intensify the hydrolysis process and methane yield, several disintegration options of WAS such as mechanical, bacterial, physical, chemical and integrated disintegration methods have been developed and implemented so far [6]. Of these, bacterial disintegration is an ecologically safe method to persuade efficient solubilisation without any hazardous substances formation. In the bacterial disintegration, the extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) of sludge hinders the available nutrient to microbes [7]. EPS protects the microbial aggregates in the sludge to prevent cell rupture and lysis. Therefore, deflocculation process, an EPS removal technique that helps to weaken the microbial aggregates for promoting floc disruption and exposes the microbial cell for bacterial disintegration [8].

Deflocculation techniques employed in WAS are chemical (alkaline chemicals, cation binding agents and AOP chemicals), physical (Thermal and ultrasonication) and mechanical (disperser) method. The chemical method of deflocculation is preferred mostly owing to its effective extrication of exopolymer within short time duration The chemical method utilizes alkaline chemical such as NaOH, KOH, NaCl, CaCl2 etc., cation binding agents such as sodium citrate, citric acid etc., and AOP chemicals such as TiO2, Fenton, H2O2 etc., and various other chemicals [9]. Advanced oxidation using photocatalysis is a high potent eco-remediation process that involved in organic pollutants deterioration. It also disintegrates and deflocculates the microbial activity of sludge and aids in digestion. This green technique makes use of certain metal oxides as photocatalyst namely: CuO, SiO2, TiO2, ZnO, etc., to perform deflocculation process [10]. Among these photocatalysts, TiO2 holds high potency with good photo-oxidation property and offers less cost and photo-induced non-toxic organic degradation [11]. On illuminating this TiO2 to solar radiation, the valence band electrons shifted to the conduction band and result in the creation of energized holes. Then, this energized hole reacts with water or hydroxyl ion, which leads to the formation of hydroxyl radicals. This high oxidative hydroxyl radical involved in the decomposition of the sludge [12]. Usage of suspended photocatalyst for sludge treatment has certain drawbacks such as catalyst aggregation, catalytic slurry formation and inherent cost for separation of catalyst from the sludge. In addition, suspended photocatalyst induces sludge turbidity and causes light shadowing effect that becomes an obstacle for photocatalytic activity [13]. These drawbacks pressurize the suspended photocatalysts as an inadequate substance for sludge remediation. To overcome this limitation, photocatalytic immobilization on fixed support as thin film and impregnation of photocatalyst on solid matrix came into existence to improve photocatalyst performance. Certain research reports regarding the utilization of the immobilized photocatalysts include the TiO2 deposited on circulating bed photocatalytic reactor for sludge pretreatment [14], Pretreatment of sludge using Ag/TiO2 coated photocatalytic reactor [15], and the MoS2/Ag/TiO2 coated nanocomposite photocatalytic film for efficient disintegration of organics [16]. Most recently, impregnating photocatalyst on polymeric substances are widely used to form nanocomposite film that exhibits multifunctional behavior. This nanocomposite film effectually inhibits photocatalytic adherence with recoverability, reusability and compatibility. Herein present investigation, an effort to disperse sludge aggregates using TiO2/chitosan nanocomposite thin film (TCTF) was made. The researchers has not documented any report of TCTF usage in sludge deflocculation until now. The main objective of the study are (i) impregnation of TiO2 on the chitosan to form TCTF for effective photocatalytic activity, (ii) to evaluate the proficiency of TCTF in sludge deflocculation, with negligible microbial stress, (iii) to assess the potency of TCTF on enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration, (iv) to predict the impact of TCTF mediated enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration on biomethane generation (v) to predict the commercial viability of the proposed sludge management method on large scale.

Municipal wastewater treatment plant situated in Trivandrum, Kerala produces a large amount of Municipal Waste Activated Sludge (WAS). This WAS was sampled from the recirculation line of secondary sedimentation tank. To hinder bacterial activity, the sampled WAS was preserved in the laboratory at 4 °C. The physicochemical characteristics of WAS were analysed and was tabulated in Table 1 .

ce:section.ce:section-title: Exopolymer (EPS) extraction protocol using TiO2 (in suspension)
ce:section.ce:para: Solar photocatalytic process using TiO2 (in suspension) was performed in 7 similar glass trays. To this each tray, 300 mL of sludge was taken and different dosages of TiO2 (0.01 to 0.1 g/g SS) was added to each tray. These trays were kept under the solar radiation. The samples were collected at a constant time of 15 min. The collected samples were centrifuged at 7500 rpm for 15 min. Then, supernatant is collected and analysed for the estimation of protein, carbohydrate and DNA to optimize the dosage of TiO2.

ce:section.ce:section-title: TiO2 embedded chitosan thin film (TCTF) preparation
ce:section.ce:para: The TCTF was formed based on the procedure of Senthil Kumar et al., [17]. A nanocomposite solution was prepared by the addition of commercial TiO2 nanoparticles (optimized previously) into 1% of glacial acetic acid. The solution was mixed for about 10 min and then chitosan powder was added and mixed vigorously to attain the homogeneous form and then sonicated for 15mins. In the reaction mixture, 0.1 M NaOH was added until the pH reached 6.0. Then the homogeneous mixture was poured into a Petridish and was dried at room temperature. Further, the film was dried in an oven at 50 °C and subsequently dried film was peeled off from the petridish

A 300 mL of sludge was taken in a 1 L glass tray. Then the optimized dosage of TiO2 embedded chitosan thin film (TCTF) was placed on the sludge and kept under the solar radiation for 1 h. The samples were collected at different intervals of time from the tray which ranges from 5 min to 60 min. Centrifugation of the collected samples was carried out at 7500 rpm for 15 min. The supernatants of the centrifuged samples were filtered and analysed for exopolymers to optimize the solar irradiation time for waste activated sludge deflocculation.

After deflocculatiion, 250 mL of conical flask was taken and utilized for performing enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration. The bacterium used in the study was Bacillus jerish 03 (Accession number: KC597266) and Bacillus jerish 04 (Accession number: KC597267) which was isolated and identified as per the earlier research [18]. Three conical flasks: control (200 mL of raw sludge), flocculated [raw sludge (200 mL) + bacteria (1 g dry cell weight/L)] and deflocculated [deflocculated sludge (200 mL) + bacteria (1 g dry cell weight/L)]. The experiment was carried out to assess the efficacy of this proposed disintegration. Incubation of whole sludge samples at 40 °C was done under constant mixing upto 42 h maintaining 6.5 pH. The sample were collected and periodic analysis of SS, SCOD and biopolymer release were done at regular time intervals.

300 mL of serum bottle has been used for batch anaerobic test to calculate the bioenergy (methane) production which was executed in accordance with the method illustrated by [19]. These investigations were done in mesophilic condition (37 ± 1 °C). The evaluation of anaerobic biomethanation test was taken for all three samples (control flocculated and deflocculated sludge). The maintained inoculum and substrate ratio was 3:1. The inoculum used is bovine rumin fluid and the substrate used are sludge samples. In order to have better compliance and scare endogenous respiration, the inoculum must be active [20]. Proper measuring of methane production was done by the syringe and needle arrangement. A comparative study of the enhanced methane generation of different sludge samples were carried out. The kinetic study of methane generation was analysed by first-order kinetic model and the specific methane production rate was evaluated. From the pilot-scale study, preliminary assessment of economic feasibility prior to the implementation of the proposed treatment process is mandatory [22]. The energy and cost analysis are focussed in this aspect to evaluate the efficiency of the proposed treatment using the experimental data obtained. Hence, about 1 ton of sludge was used for analysis. The input energy spent for the sludge treatment was pumping of the sludge, mechanical stirring utilized for deflocculation, pretreatment and anaerobic digestion. Table 2 details the parameters and assumed data during the proposed method of energetic, solid and cost analysis.

In cost analysis, the energy cost (EC) incurred during the implementing the treatment, utilized chemicals cost (CC), the cost that is to be spent for remained solid disposal, cost gained in solid reduction due to the proposed sludge management process were taken into consideration. In accordance with the research of Kavitha et al., [18] the cost required for one kWh of energy was $0.23 and correspondingly the cost incurred for per kg of solid was $ 0.28 for solid reduced and disposed. The cost of methane in the form of energy and reduced cost for sludge disposal (RSDC) in the treatment process was measured as a positive cost (gain). The cost spent for chemical utilization, cost of total energy applied for the treatment and cost of the solid remained after treatment for disposal was considered as negative cost (loss). The net profit (NP) was evaluated by deducting the loss from gain cost.

Entire analysis was executed in triplicate and attained output was revealed as a mean of three values. Student t test vs one way analysis of variance was preferred to assess the results significance. The results are thought to be statistically significant when the value of p < 0.05.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Optimization of TiO2 in suspension for film preparation
ce:section.ce:para:
Prior to impregnation of photocatalyst (TiO2) on chitosan solid matrix, the photocatalytic process performed using various suspended TiO2 dosage (0.01 g/g SS to 0.1 g/g SS) to optimize its usage for preparing TCTF. From (Fig. 1a
), it was observed that the concentration of biopolymer release i.e., protein, carbohydrate and DNA augments gradually from 14.35 to 43.54 mg/L, 9.11 to 30.76 mg/L and 4.25 to 24.39 mg/L, respectively when the TiO2 dosage was 0.05 g/g SS. This gradual increment illustrates the disruption of adhered microbial cell within the sludge which induces the release of exopolymers without any microbial stress [24]. DNA release confirmed the deflocculation process since the DNA release was minimal up to 0.05 g/g SS and hikes rapidly when the dosage increases beyond it. A tremendous increment of DNA from 55 mg/L to 104.40 mg/L up to the dosage of 0.1 g/g SS TiO2 dosage. This explains the secretion of intracellular medium due to microbial lysis. The disruption of exopolymer without microbial lysis was a significant aspect during deflocculation process. This change of phase from deflocculation to disintegration was detailed in the figure by linear profile. The gradual linear increment indicates the deflocculation phase and rapid increment of biopolymer release indicates the disintegration phase. Hence, 0.05 g/g SS an optimal dosage effectively deflocculates the sludge and used for film preparation.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Deflocculation using TiO2 embedded chitosan thin film (TCTF)
ce:section.ce:para: Exopolymer (EPS) exist in the sludge matrix was excreted by microbes during its period of growth. This double-layered exopolymer [(Loosely bound (Lb) and tightly bound (Tb) layer] promotes sludge stability and matrix structure by aggregation that can be large or dense [25]. This promotes firm floc structure. Loosely bound is the outermost layer, which diffuses through the tightly bound EPS. Microbial cell available in outer flocs structure entangled thinly to LB-EPS. Disruption of this exopolymer increases the bioavailability of microbial cell for further disintegration process [26]. In this study, TCTF effectively deflocculates the sludge exopolymers. The variation in the exopolymers subfractions (bound and extractable EPS), biopolymers, DNA and exoenzyme release assist in the determination of deflocculation efficacy of TCTF.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Variation in DNA release and exopolymer fraction
ce:section.ce:para:
(Fig. 1b
) details the variation of exopolymer fractions using TCTF. The observed concentration of Lb and Tb in the raw sludge was 30.2 mg/L and 20.08 mg/L respectively. TCTF disperses the microbial cell and expels the exopolymers from the double-layered sludge floc structure to the aqueous phase. The extractable EPS was estimated to be 50.28 mg/L by summing the bound exopolymers. Bound EPS profile was distinguished into two phases of declination: positive decline and negative decline. The positive decline was from 0 to 50 min. In this declination, a rapid reduction in the bound EPS (Lb – 20 to 0.5 mg/L and Tb – 30 to 0 mg/L) was seen with the subsequent increment and decrement in extractable EPS. The increment in extractable EPS (6 mg/L to 50.07 mg/L) was found up to 25 min due to the release of exopolymers with corresponding increment in concentration of DNA from 6.54 mg/L to 24.41 mg/L. The maximum deflocculation efficiency of 99.35% was achieved at 25 min. Decreased extractable EPS indicates the degradation of exopolymeric substances and the corresponding DNA decrement from 19.17 mg/L to 0.42 mg/L at 50 min due to the complete degradation of released extracellular substances. When the time exceeds 50 min, the negative decline was seen in bound EPS. This specifies the solubilisation of particulate organics to aqueous phase for enhancing intracellular substance release. This could be evident from the extractable EPS and DNA variation from 40.45 mg/L to 98.67 mg/L and 25.70 mg/L to 65.64 mg/L, respectively. This sudden rise of DNA highlights the cell lysis. The effective disruption of microbial cell with any cell lysis could be seen at the duration of 25 min which is considered to be an optimum time for deflocculation.

Exoenzyme release and its activity was assessed during deflocculation and its variation was elucidated in (Fig. 1b ). From the figure, the activities of exoenzyme increases from 0.02 U/mL to 0.44 U/mL (protease) and 0 U/mL to 0.38 U/mL (amylase) with the increment in treatment time upto 25 min. This signifies the release of entangled enzymes during floc disruption [20]. Beyond 25 min, enzyme activity decreased (protease- 0.38 to 0 U/mL and amylase- 0.36 to 0 U/mL) owing to the degradation of released exopolymers. However, a further sudden rise in the enzyme activity beyond 50 min indicates the abrupt release of intracellular enzyme due to cell lysis. Thus, deflocculation time of 25 min was optimal to promote better disruption of exopolymer.

ce:section.ce:section-title: TCTF mediated enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration
ce:section.ce:para: During sludge disintegration, the inoculated bacteria strain releases protease and amylase enzymes to induce biomass stress. This biomass stress promotes cell cleavage that causes solubilisation of particulate organic to aqueous phase. TCTF mediated bacterial disintegration enables easy accessibility of substrate to the microbes and surface area increment for better solubilisation. Time is the major parameter to enhance and achieve a better disintegration process. This study details the role of enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration in raw sludge and TCTF treated sludge.

The released intracellular stuff protein and carbohydrate during disintegration was depicted in (Fig. 3
). The plot of protein and carbohydrate was in conformity with the SCOD release plot. As explained in SCOD plot, the variation of protein was increasing up to 42 h from 0 to 6.88 mg/L, 0 to 246.96 mg/L, 0 to 452.48 mg/L, respectively for control, flocculated and deflocculated sludge. Similarly, carbohydrate release increased from 0 mg/L to 44.28 mg/L, 158.76 mg/L and 290.88 mg/L, respectively for control, flocculated and deflocculated sludge. Beyond 42 h, decrement of intracellular stuffs within the sludge. This decrement might be the degradation of protein into amino acids and peptides by protease enzyme and carbohydrate degradation to simple sugar by amylase enzyme [29]. Increment in release of protein and carbohydrates was due to cell lysis. A decrement in protein and carbohydrate indicates the non-availability of substrate for inoculated substrate that promotes depletion of the released intracellular stuff. On Comparative analysis, control exhibited trivial protein and carbohydrate due to the presence of solubilised and particulate organics. In addition, the solubilisation was higher in deflocculated sludge due to the dispersion of the microbial cell and exopolymer removal. Maximum protein, carbohydrate and SCOD release of 452.48 mg/L, 290.88 mg/L and 808 mg/L, respectively was achieved in deflocculated sludge under the optimized disintegration time of 42 h. This implies the complete release of intracellular substances. The p-value calculated during the standard T test for protein and carbohydrate were found to be 0.021 and 0.022 which is less than 0.05 and implies the significant difference between flocculated and deflocculated sludge.

ce:section.ce:para:

The selective medium used in the current research was skimmed milk agar according to the description provided in [2]. The inoculated bacteria used to disintegrate was plated on a skimmed agar medium for secreting protease strain to form colonies which was counted for each time interval. The solid balance of the proposed method was shown in (Fig. 6 ). The overall solid decreased in the sludge treatment was 306.25, and 478 kg for flocculated and deflocculated sludge, respectively. Overall solid reduction of 47.8% was achieved during anaerobic digestion of TCTF mediated bacterial disintegration. Of these, anaerobic digestion alone reduced 23.1% and 34.8% of solids for flocculated and deflocculated sludge. The net solid for disposal in this proposed work was predicted to be 693.75 and 522 kg, correspondingly for the flocculated and deflocculated samples. About 77.01 and 33.62% of solid has been reduced in the deflocculated sludge than the control and flocculated sludge samples, respectively. Maximum solid reduced in deflocculated sludge via landfill and fetches revenue by decreasing the cost required for landfilling.

The net cost (NC) of the flocculated and deflocculated sample were assessed to be USD (35.96, and 89.92). Cost analysis detailed the cost spent for consumables and solids to be disposed. TCTF can be reused which resulted in negligible consumable cost. Also, it restricts the availability of photocatalysts in the effluent stream during disposal which enables easy disposal of sludge directly after this proposed management process. About 0.28 USD cost was utilized for disposing per kg of sludge. The output energy obtained as methane gained 0.23 USD/kWh. The cost of profitable methane energy during flocculated and deflocculated sludge was 51.75 and 107.74 USD respectively. The high net cost of the proposed method of treatment was achieved in deflocculated samples. It is understandable from the above findings that the TCTF mediated enzyme secreting bacterial pretreatment can be a better option for sludge management with high energy ratio of 1.05. The net profit of the proposed treatment method was comparatively higher than that of net profit of Chi et al., [33] and Park et al., [34] which was about 83.39 and 21.54 USD/Ton of sludge respectively during anaerobic digestion of the pretreated sludge. Also, Ushani et al., [30] performed similar phase separated bacterial pretreatment and achieved net profit of only 2.6 USD/ton of sludge. Sun et al., [35] earned 68.57 USD/t of sludge as net profit in hydrocyclone pretreatment. An overall comparative study has drawn and concluded that the proposed treatment method was profitable at large scale.

At present, air purifications using TiO2 photocatalytic are in practice. Its utilization in the field of wastewater and sludge treatment has gained higher importance because of non-toxic by-products. Numerous laboratorial research regarding the usage of TiO2 in wastewater and waste activated sludge (WAS) treatment is still in demo scale. The research on photocatalytic thin film utilization for sludge treatment was a growing technology. Performance evaluation of reusability thin film photocatalyst requires more investigation is forthcoming. Also, detailed examination of thin film surface deviation analysis was obligatory. Hence, a broad investigation is necessary to push this process to large scale.

The potency of TCTF mediated enzyme secreting bacterial disintegration was estimated by biomethanation analysis. The flocculated and deflocculated sludge efficiently liberates maximum intracellular organic stuff (Protein – 246.96 mg/L flocculated and 452.42 mg/L deflocculated; Carbohydrate – 158.76 mg/L flocculated and 290.88 mg/L deflocculated) within the microbial cell at 42 h of disintegration time. But, deflocculated sludge showed more solubilisation (16%) and solid reduction (12.5%) which increases the substrate accessibility further treatment process. An enhanced bioenergy production of 0.32 gCOD/gCOD was recorded in deflocculated sludge having 89.92 USD/Ton of sludge as net profit at an accessible level.
